findings.text: Two virtualization helpers are globally visible for broadcast and control. One asks all virtual CPUs in a VM to scan IOAPIC state. The other sets or clears a reason indexed APIC virtualization inhibit under lock.

Two Xen helpers are globally visible. One injects a pending Xen upcall as a local APIC interrupt. The other reports whether the cached Xen info block signals a pending upcall, handling validation and refresh.
Four memory helpers are globally visible. One validates a cached guest to host mapping. One refreshes that mapping. One converts a user address to a frame number. One releases a clean page reference.
Two small inline wrappers provide set and clear entry points for APIC virtualization inhibits. Each delegates to the global setter with a boolean that selects set versus clear for the given reason.
Inhibit updates are serialized by a write lock held in the VM architecture state. The global setter returns early when the feature is disabled and otherwise holds the lock across the inner update.

Physical map construction enforces a strict one to one relation between physical identifiers and virtual CPUs when wide identifier format is off, failing on alias. When wide format is on, extended mode entries and large identifiers use the extended slot while legacy entries fill the low slot only when empty, tolerating wrap alias.

Identifier bounds and aliasing need care. Oversize legacy identifiers warn and fail without killing the VM. Oversize extended identifiers signal that the map grew stale due to concurrent addition or enable. Mismatch detection truncates the virtual CPU identifier to the low byte so large values do not falsely report mismatch, with later alias checks catching real collisions.

Logical map construction unifies mode across software enabled APICs. The first such APIC fixes the map mode. A later APIC with a different mode disables the optimized map. Disabled software state and empty destination leave the map unchanged.

Extended logical mode needs no extra cluster work because the destination derives from the extended identifier and reuses the physical map. Legacy flat and cluster modes resolve a cluster table plus mask, ignore empty masks, and disable the map when the mask has more than one bit or the target slot is already occupied.

Writing the software vector register updates the stored value and tracks software enable transitions. A change updates a global disabled indicator and marks the APIC map dirty. An enable also requests page ready processing and invokes the Xen enable hook.

Writing the legacy identifier or the logical destination or the destination format marks the APIC map dirty, so the next use rebuilds the optimized tables. The identifier write shifts the low byte into the architectural position.

The active Xen enable hook injects only when the global Xen feature is on and the per virtual CPU info cache is active and an upcall vector is configured and the pending flag reads set. The alternate build variant is an empty no operation.

Xen vector injection builds a fixed physical interrupt directed at the requesting virtual CPU identifier with no shorthand and asserted level, using the configured Xen upcall vector, then delivers it through the local APIC path.

Xen pending detection reads one flag byte from the cached guest info block. It first validates layout compatibility at build time, then loops validating the cache, refreshing outside the read lock when stale, reporting pending when in atomic or non running context to force a wake, and reporting none when userspace broke the mapping.

Xen pending detection holds an interrupt saving read lock while validating the cache and loading the flag byte. It drops the lock before any refresh that might sleep and reacquires it before rechecking.

Cache validation requires an active cache with a non error user address and a set valid flag and a length that fits in one page. Caches backed by a guest address also require a current memory slot generation.

Length fit means the offset inside the page plus the requested length stays within the page. The offset comes from the user address when the guest address holds the error sentinel and otherwise from the guest address.

The refresh entry point guards the cache with a scoped mutex, rejects lengths that would cross a page boundary, ignores the stored user address for guest backed caches, and delegates to the inner refresh with exactly one valid address kind.

Refresh uses two levels. The outer mutex is held across the whole operation and asserted in helpers. The inner write interrupt lock protects fields and is dropped around user to frame lookup and kernel mapping that may sleep, then reacquired before publishing.

Inner refresh rejects use when inactive and rejects dual valid or dual invalid addresses. Guest backed refresh updates generation and slot and user address when the guest address or generation changed. User backed refresh clears slot state and tracks user address change. Unchanged user address with a still valid mapping only adjusts for the new page offset. Changed mapping does a fresh lookup. Failure clears validity and the frame and kernel address while keeping address metadata.

The retry helper clears validity before dropping the lock, samples the invalidation sequence, looks up the frame and kernel mapping without the lock, then rechecks for concurrent invalidation under the lock. A race discards the attempt and releases resources and reschedules opportunistically. Success publishes the frame and offset adjusted kernel address and marks the entry valid.

The mapping cache carries active and valid flags plus guest address and page aligned user address and memory slot pointer and generation and frame number and kernel address, with an owning VM reference and a refresh mutex and an interrupt aware read write lock.

The address resolution descriptor carries a slot pointer and guest frame and flags and user address and an output slot for a referenced page, with optional pin request and optional writable map reporting. Resolution records the page or tracker result and reports writability when asked.

Fast user to frame lookup applies only when the caller asks for write or writable mapping, avoiding a race with copy on write for read only intents. It uses a pinned fast path when pinning is requested and an unpinned fast path otherwise, resolving the page to a frame on hit.

Slow lookup adds poison and NUMA hint handling to caller flags, pins or gets one page, and opportunistically upgrades a read fault to writable when allowed and not pinning. Remapped areas go through a tracker with fault fixup and retry when the lock was dropped, while ordinary areas validate read and write permissions and report distinct error frames for fault versus needs IO.

Remapped handling refuses pinning when unsafe mappings are disallowed. It starts address tracking, fixes a user fault when tracking has not started, retries when the fix dropped the lock, fails read only frames on write faults, and otherwise resolves through the tracker.
Page release helpers tolerate a null pointer. The clean variant marks the page accessed before dropping the reference, but only for pages that are not reserved for special use.

Kernel mapping prefers a direct page map when the frame is valid. When not valid it uses an input output remap with write back caching where the platform supports input output memory, and otherwise reports failure with a null address.
Host physical address is derived from the frame number shifted by the page shift. Error guest addresses are recognized by equality with an invalid sentinel.

Invalidation retry first checks an active invalidation count and then compares the sampled sequence with the current sequence under ordering that pairs with the range end barrier, so either a concurrent start or a completed increment forces a retry.

Stale physical maps and mixed logical modes must disable optimization rather than misdeliver. Concurrent enable between allocation and calculation is detected through the extended bound. Wrapped low identifiers and duplicated cluster bits force fallback to the slow path.

Cache refresh must not sleep while holding the inner write lock and must detect frame change before dropping it. The old kernel mapping is unmapped only after unlock. A new lookup that reuses the same frame keeps the old mapping to avoid needless churn.

Distinct failures are signaled by standard codes. Invalid argument covers oversize legacy identifiers and aliased physical entries and bad refresh lengths and dual address misuse and inactive use. Too big covers stale extended maps. Fault covers untranslatable guest addresses and failed frame lookups.

Local APIC architectural selectors observed here include the software vector and identifier and logical destination and destination format registers, flat versus cluster encodings, physical destination with no shorthand and fixed delivery, and logical mode tags for disabled and software disabled and flat and cluster and extended operation.
